extracted.intended_audience: readers interested in mathematical creativity (mathematicians, cognitive psychologists, historians/philosophers of science, and educated general readers)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and explicating Poincaré's criteria and observations about how mathematical invention occurs — the roles of conscious work, unconscious thought, aesthetic sensibility, and conditions that produce sudden insight. Useful for analyzing or reproducing mathematical-creativity processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creation = choice of useful combinations
rubrics_metrics.description: “To create consists precisely in not making useless combinations and in making those which are useful and which are only a small minority. Invention is discernment, choice.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poincaré frames invention as selective: the creative act is identified with avoiding the vast bulk of useless combinations and producing the few useful ones. He emphasizes that the rules guiding this choice are extremely fine and delicate and cannot be mechanically stated; they are felt more than formulated. Anti-pattern: treating creativity as brute-force combinatorics (trying all combinations) rather than selective discernment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical facts worthy of study reveal mathematical laws by analogy
rubrics_metrics.description: “The mathematical facts worthy of being studied are those which, by their analogy with other facts, are capable of leading us to the knowledge of a mathematical law just as experimental facts lead us to the knowledge of a physical law.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion for 'usefulness'—a fact is valuable if it indicates deeper law-like structure via analogy to other known facts. When evaluating candidate results, prefer those that suggest generalizable laws. Example: Poincaré sought combinations revealing kinship between previously separate facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fertile combinations often draw elements from distant domains
rubrics_metrics.description: “Among chosen combinations the most fertile will often be those formed of elements drawn from domains which are far apart.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourages cross-domain association as a source of creativity, but with a caveat: arbitrarily disparate combinations are usually sterile; only rare cross-domain matches are highly fruitful. Guidance: look for analogies across distant areas, but expect most such attempts to fail; successful ones are rare and particularly valuable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long unconscious prior work culminates in sudden illumination
rubrics_metrics.description: Poincaré reports repeated anecdotes: after many days of fruitless conscious effort the solution 'comes entirely from its own accord' later during rest, walking, or unrelated activity; sudden idea is brief, certain, and accompanied by feeling of illumination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat sudden insights as the visible result of extended unconscious processing. Example: Poincaré’s discovery moments for Fuchsian functions occurred while walking, travelling, or after sleep. When judging creative episodes, consider the preceding period of effort as part of the causal chain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fruitful unconscious processing must be preceded by conscious work
rubrics_metrics.description: “It is possible, and of a certainty it is only fruitful, if it is on the one hand preceded and on the other hand followed by a period of conscious work.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conscious effort primes the unconscious: directed attempts mobilize the relevant 'elements' so unconscious recombination has a reasonable search space. Practical implication: planning and deliberate work should precede rest/ incubation periods. Anti-pattern: expecting incubation to produce results without prior problem-directed effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sudden inspiration requires subsequent conscious verification and elaboration
rubrics_metrics.description: Poincaré stresses that after inspiration 'the second period of conscious work' is necessary to put the inspiration in shape, deduce consequences, write demonstrations, and verify; the feeling of certainty can be deceptive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat inspirations as hypotheses or starting points, not finished proofs. Always follow insight with disciplined verification, calculation, and formalization. Example: Poincaré felt certainty on a walk but only verified and wrote out the results later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic (emotional) sensibility acts as the sieve selecting unconscious outputs
rubrics_metrics.description: Poincaré proposes that the privileged unconscious phenomena are those that 'affect most profoundly our emotional sensibility' and that mathematical beauty/harmony helps the geometer recognize useful combinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion for what surfaces to consciousness: candidate ideas that evoke a sense of mathematical beauty are more likely to be considered and developed. Practical use: cultivate aesthetic judgment to help filter promising avenues. Anti-pattern: ignoring aesthetic responses as irrelevant to mathematical value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two hypotheses on the unconscious’s role: discernment vs. automatic production plus selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Poincaré contrasts (1) the subliminal self as capable of discernment and choosing useful combinations, and (2) the subliminal self as automatic, producing many combinations but only the interesting ones break into consciousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When modeling unconscious creativity, consider both possibilities: either the unconscious has selective capacity or consciousness performs the selection (via aesthetic/emotional response). Evaluate evidence (e.g., frequency of false inspirations) to distinguish which applies in context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unconscious inspirations are usually brief, sudden, and accompanied by vivid certainty but can mislead
rubrics_metrics.description: Poincaré notes inspirations come with 'brevity, suddenness and immediate certainty' yet sometimes 'this feeling deceives us'—particularly in hypnagogic states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat subjective certainty as provisional. Insist on empirical/mathematical verification even when the insight feels undeniably true. Beware of hypnagogic/marginal states producing plausible but false ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unconscious processing typically does not perform long mechanical calculations
rubrics_metrics.description: Poincaré observes that unconscious work never produces 'the result of a somewhat long calculation all made'; it provides only a point of departure for subsequent conscious computation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not expect incubation to deliver completed algorithmic or arithmetical work; plan to perform systematic calculations and verifications consciously after inspiration. Use insight to set up the right calculation rather than to replace it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Environmental change and rest facilitate unconscious problem solving
rubrics_metrics.description: Poincaré’s anecdotes show solutions appearing during travel, walking, at the seaside, or after sleep; he contrasts 'complete repose' with periods of unconscious work in which ideas are mobilized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical condition: incorporate breaks, changes of scene, and rest into problem-solving routine to allow unconscious recombination. Anti-pattern: continuous forced work without breaks, which can fail to trigger unconscious processing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary conscious work 'mobilizes' relevant elements and reduces search space
rubrics_metrics.description: Using the 'hooked atoms' metaphor: conscious work detaches and mobilizes certain elements so they can meet and combine during unconscious activity; will-directed mobilization is not random and targets promising elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberate exploration should aim to identify and activate promising components of the problem so incubation has material to recombine. This explains why earlier 'fruitless' effort is crucial—it shapes the set of elements that unconscious processes will use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creativity requires interplay of freedom (unconscious disorder) and discipline (conscious rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poincaré contrasts the subliminal self’s 'liberty' (absence of discipline, disorder enabling unexpected combinations) with the conscious self’s need for 'discipline, attention, will' to carry out strict calculations and verifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design workflows that alternate open-ended, undirected exploration (allowing serendipity) with disciplined, rule-governed work to verify and extend results. Avoid exclusively one mode: too much freedom yields unverified chaos; too much discipline stifles novel recombinations.
